_about: How every armed conflict and military event touching Miami was actually fought, broken down for animation. Coordinates are approximate (WGS84) and meant for placement in the 3D scene, not surveying. confidence: high = confirmed by 2+ independent sources; medium = single source or inferred from confirmed facts (the inference is stated); low = plausible but unconfirmed, verify before animating. 'do_not_show' lists things that would be historically wrong.
_global_note: Miami has NEVER been bombed from the air and no air-to-air or air-to-ground combat ever happened over the city. Military aircraft appear only as training flights, anti-submarine patrols, blimp convoy escorts (1942-45), alert/scramble fighters and reconnaissance jets heading south toward Cuba (1962), and one disguised B-26 landing at Miami International Airport (1961). Animate jets as patrols, take-offs and fly-overs, never as attacks on Miami.

sequences.title: The Spanish arrive / the mission fails

sides.forces: Pedro Menendez de Aviles' expedition; in March 1567 a mission inside a stockade with 30 soldiers and Jesuit brother Francisco Villareal
sides.vessels: Small sailing vessels. Menendez sailed with 'one hundred men in three brigantines' in June 1566 on his coastal voyages; the exact ships at Tequesta are not recorded
sides.weapons: Arquebuses, swords, armour (typical Spanish kit of the period, not specifically documented here)

sides.forces: Main village at the mouth of the Miami River; population estimates at contact range from 800 to 10,000
sides.weapons: Not described in the sources gathered; verify before animating

approach.from: Havana / St. Augustine along the coast
approach.path_hint: Ships enter Biscayne Bay through the gap north of Key Biscayne (there is no Government Cut yet) and anchor off the river mouth

beats.what: Menendez lands at the Tequesta village and erects a cross
Stockade/blockhouse mission, 30 soldiers, Brother Villareal teaching children
Spanish soldiers kill (accounts say executed) an uncle of the chief; the Tequesta burn their own settlement and withdraw into the Everglades, later returning to attack the garrison
Most soldiers escape and withdraw to St. Augustine (by sea)
Mission abandoned; the Jesuits withdraw from Florida

effects: canoes paddling west up the river
do_not_show: a pitched battle with many dead: no casualty numbers are recorded
stone forts: it was a timber stockade
sequences.location_notes: Sources disagree on which bank the 1567 stockade stood on: miami-history.com says the north bank; Wikipedia (Tequesta) and Legends of America say near the south bank. See README discrepancies.

locations.name: Tequesta main village, north bank of the river mouth

sequences.title: Raids from the north and removal to Cuba

sides.side: Carolina settlers and allied Yamasee raiders
sides.forces: Raiding parties; by 1707 they had 'killed, carried off, or driven away most of the remaining native inhabitants' down the full length of the peninsula
Evacuation ships: 280 South Florida natives taken to Cuba in 1710, nearly 200 died; survivors returned to the Keys in 1716-1718

approach.medium: land and canoe from the north; Spanish evacuation by sea to Havana

beats.what: Villages emptied; population counter falls
Ships carry about 280 people to Cuba

do_not_show: a specific battle at the Miami River: no documented raid on the Miami village itself was found; show the depopulation, not a staged fight

sequences.title: The last mission (Pueblo de Santa Maria de Loreto)

sides.forces: Jesuit Fathers Joseph Maria Monaco and Joseph Xavier Alana, with men from the garrison
sides.vessels: Sent from Cuba; left June 24, 1743 and anchored at the river mouth about three weeks later (ship type not recorded)

beats.what: Ship anchors; stockade built near the water's edge
Only 180 natives live there, half of them children; the adults are hostile
Mission closed (Wikipedia's Tequesta article says it lasted less than three months)

locations.name: 1743 stockade site, near today's Southeast Financial Center (formerly Wachovia Financial Center)

sequences.title: Second Seminole War reaches the Miami River

sides.forces: Overseer James Wright, about 60 enslaved workers and local white families

approach.medium: Seminole threat by land from the interior; evacuation by boat

beats.what: By January 6, 1836 the plantation is under imminent threat
Everyone is evacuated. Many of the enslaved people did not feel threatened by the Seminoles and wanted to join them
Plantation abandoned; fields go back to scrub

do_not_show: an attack on the plantation: the sources describe a threat and evacuation, not a battle

locations.name: Fitzpatrick plantation, north bank of the Miami River

sequences.title: Attack on the Cape Florida Lighthouse
sequences.type: raid / siege of a single tower
sequences.in_main_frame: wide frame only (Key Biscayne, about 12 km south of downtown)

sides.forces: A raiding band (Thompson's account as reported: about 12 Seminoles in 'the sloop'; other retellings say 30-40, so the number is disputed)
sides.vessels: Arrived by water; Key Biscayne is an island. One account mentions a sloop; canoes are likely too (inferred)

sides.forces: Assistant keeper John W. B. Thompson and Aaron Carter, a Black handyman. Carter was killed
sides.weapons: Rifle/muskets, balls, a keg of gunpowder

sides.vessels: Navy schooner Motto, then men from the schooner Pee Dee the next day

approach.to: Cape Florida, south tip of Key Biscayne

beats.what: Seminoles surround the tower; rifle balls go through Thompson's clothes and hat
Raiders set fire to the door and a boarded-up ground-floor window; bullets pierce the tanks holding 225 gallons of lamp oil, which ignites
Thompson and Carter climb to the top with rifle, balls and a powder keg, cutting away part of the wooden stairs below them
Thompson throws the keg down the burning tower; it explodes but the tower stands. Carter dies
Believing both men dead, the raiders pillage the keeper's house and leave
Motto heard the blast 12 miles away; the next day its crew and men from the Pee Dee fire a ramrod tied to a line up to Thompson and haul him down

effects: flames climbing the inside of the tower (glow in the windows)
sequences.aftermath: The light stays dark for 10 years; it is repaired in 1846 and relit in April 1847

sequences.title: Fort Dallas and the Navy's 'Mosquito Fleet'

sides.forces: Summer 1836: Lt. L. M. Powell lands at the river mouth and builds blockhouses; post named after Commodore Alexander J. Dallas. From Oct 1, 1838 to Aug 3, 1842 Lt. John T. McLaughlin's Florida Squadron, based on Key Biscayne and Indian Key
sides.vessels: Schooners (e.g. USS Flirt, flagship from Dec 1839) on Biscayne Bay patrols to stop trade between the Seminoles and Cuba/West Indies; canoes and flat-bottomed boats for joint Army-Navy Everglades expeditions

sides.forces: Army unit at Fort Dallas October 1839 to January 1842; Col. William S. Harney commanded 1839-1840

approach.medium: sea (schooners patrolling the bay) + river (canoes going west up the Miami River)

beats.what: Blockhouses and barracks appear at the river mouth
Schooners cruise Biscayne Bay; canoe flotillas head up the river

locations.name: Fort Dallas (original site, north bank near the river mouth)

sequences.title: Harney's canoe raid into the Everglades
sequences.in_main_frame: departure and return only; the fight itself is deep in the Everglades, off-map

sides.forces: Col. William S. Harney with 90 men in 16 canoes; guided by a Black man named John who had been held captive by the Seminoles
sides.tactics: Soldiers dressed as Indians; dawn surprise attack

sides.forces: Camp on an island in the Everglades

approach.to: West up the Miami River, over the rapids, into the Everglades

beats.what: 16 canoes paddle west from Fort Dallas
Dawn surprise; Chakaika shot while offering his hand; 4 killed in action, 5 hanged; Harney loses 1 soldier
Back at Fort Dallas after 12 days

effects: line of canoes on the river

beats.what: US troops occupy Fort Dallas (about 15 months, uneventful)
Reestablished for the Third Seminole War (1855-1858); William English's 1844 limestone slave quarters used as Army barracks
War ends; site left uninhabited again

locations.name: Fort Dallas stone barracks (original site; moved to Lummus Park in 1924)

sequences.title: Civil War: the light goes dark
sequences.type: sabotage and blockade, no battle at Miami

sides.what: In 1861 they destroyed the Cape Florida lamp and smashed the Fresnel lens prisms so blockade runners could slip past in the dark (Jupiter light also darkened)
Union blockade of the coast; the former Fort Dallas was re-occupied by Union forces
sides.vessels: Blockading steam gunboats (e.g. USS Sagamore operated on Florida's east coast; ships specific to Biscayne Bay not found)

beats.what: Lighthouse beam switches off
A Union gunboat offshore; small blockade-running sailboats at night
Light repaired; keeper Temple Pent reappointed

do_not_show: a battle at Miami: none is recorded

sequences.title: 1898: Fort Brickell and Camp Miami
sequences.type: coastal defence + training camp, no combat

sides.forces: Fort Robert W. Davis ('Fort Brickell'), begun April 5, 1898: an earth bunker 45 ft in diameter and 20 ft high with a wooden magazine; planned for 4 guns, only 2 heavy guns mounted; garrison of about 200 'Miami Minutemen' volunteers
Camp Miami, from June 24, 1898: more than 7,000 volunteers from Alabama, Louisiana and Texas
sides.arrival: By train on the Florida East Coast Railway. The camp adjoined the FEC station and the railroad was the only overland route (inferred)

beats.what: Round earth bunker rises on the bay at Brickell
Trains arrive; rows of white tents fill the north side of downtown
War ends unofficially; no soldier trained here saw combat; tents cleared, fort disarmed

locations.name: Fort Brickell (east of Brickell Ave and SE 18th Rd, facing the bay)
Camp Miami (Biscayne Blvd to NW 2nd Ave, south edge NE 2nd St)

sequences.title: World War II: U-boats, blimps and a city in uniform
sequences.type: naval / anti-submarine war offshore; mass military training onshore
sequences.in_main_frame: partly: Miami Beach, Bayfront, the bay. The tanker sinking is about 20 km SE, off Fowey Rocks; the blimp base, Homestead and Opa-locka are off-map

sides.forces: U-boats off the Florida coast; 24 ships sunk in Florida waters during the war
sides.vessels: U-564 (Reinhard Suhren) sank the Mexican tanker Potrero del Llano; U-106 sank Faja de Oro on May 20, 1942; U-134 shot down blimp K-74 on July 18, 1943 in the Florida Straits

sides.forces: Gulf Sea Frontier (Feb 1942; HQ in Miami's DuPont Building from June 1942). Submarine Chaser Training Center at Pier 2, Bayfront (March 1942). NAS Richmond blimp base (Sept 15, 1942; squadron ZP-21 from Oct 1942; 25 K-class blimps, 3 wooden hangars 16.5 storeys high and over 1,000 ft long; 3,000 men). NAS Miami at Opa-locka: advanced fighter school
sides.vessels: Wooden subchasers and PC patrol craft (crews of 3 officers + 24 enlisted); USS PC-536 rescued the Potrero del Llano survivors
sides.aircraft: K-class blimps (convoy escort over the Florida Straits); at NAS Miami: Brewster F2A Buffalo, Grumman F4F Wildcat, Douglas SBD Dauntless, Grumman TBF Avenger (training)

sides.forces: Miami Beach Training Center (Feb 1942): the Army leased almost all of Miami Beach's hotels (more than 300 hotels and apartment buildings); nearly half a million men trained; golf courses and parks became drill fields. Miami's 36th Street Airport: ferry route from June 1941 (Air Transport Command). Homestead Army Air Field (Sept 1942): C-46, C-54, C-87 transport training

beats.what: Early 1942: Miami stays lit for tourism; ships offshore are silhouetted against the glow
Soldiers marching on the beach and golf course; hotel windows lit as barracks
Coastal blackout/dim-out ordered; the city goes dark
U-564 torpedoes Potrero del Llano at 25°35'N 80°06'W. The tanker (6,132 tons of petroleum) burns; thousands watch from Miami Beach as it drifts north; 13 dead, 22 rescued by PC-536
Blimps and subchasers escort convoys; subchasers train in the bay
Hurricane: fire destroys all three Richmond hangars with 25 blimps and 368 aircraft inside

effects: burning tanker on the horizon at night with an orange sky glow
blimps (grey cigar shapes) drifting slowly offshore
do_not_show: U-boats shelling the city: no such attack happened
sequences.timing_note: uboat.net logs the attack at '07:17 hours' without a time zone. U-boat logs are usually kept in German time, which would put the attack in the local night, and eyewitnesses describe the tanker burning for hours. Treat 'night' as likely but verify.

locations.name: Potrero del Llano attack position
locations.note: about 1.5 km NW of Fowey Rocks Light

locations.name: Miami Beach Training Center drill field (municipal golf course)

sequences.title: The secret war against Castro
sequences.type: covert operations; the invasion itself happened in Cuba
sequences.in_main_frame: partly (MIA landing; exiles in Little Havana); the JM/WAVE base and boat launches are off-map

sides.forces: Brigade 2506 (formed 1960) landed at the Bay of Pigs, Cuba on April 17, 1961. JM/WAVE station (1961-1968) in Building 25 at the former NAS Richmond, run through a front company, Zenith Technical Enterprises; at its peak (late 1962-early 1963) it ran the third-largest navy in the Caribbean
sides.vessels: Mother ships Rex and Leda (Nicaraguan-flagged, based at Port Everglades and West Palm Beach) carrying fast raiding boats
sides.aircraft: April 15, 1961: after B-26 strikes on Cuban airfields, a B-26 painted in Cuban Air Force markings and deliberately shot full of holes lands at Miami International Airport; pilot Mario Zuniga poses as a 'defector'

beats.what: Single B-26 (twin piston engines) lands at MIA; press photos
The invasion fails (in Cuba, off-map)
JFK receives the brigade's flag at the Orange Bowl

do_not_show: the invasion fleet leaving from Miami: it did not; the landing force sailed from Central America (widely documented, not re-verified here)

sequences.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: 90 miles from war
sequences.in_main_frame: mostly off-map (Homestead is about 40 km SSW of downtown). Show jets flying south past the city and missile batteries on the edges

sides.aircraft: Over 181 F-100 Super Sabre fighter-bombers (31st TFW plus the 401st and 474th TFWs; '1st Provisional Air Division', over 1,600 pilots and maintainers); more than 30 F-100Ds parked in irregular patterns, fuelled, on constant alert to scramble toward Cuba; F-102 Delta Dagger interceptors; RF-101 Voodoo recon jets flying over Cuba; transports C-47, C-54, C-123, C-130; HU-16 amphibians. SAC bombers of the 19th BW were dispersed away from Homestead

sides.forces: A tent city of more than 10,000 Army troops at Homestead; 13th Artillery Group HQ arrived Oct 30, 1962. HAWK anti-aircraft batteries from October 1962 (HM-12 Old Cutler Road, HM-39 North Canal Drive, HM-59, HM-60, HM-84); Nike Hercules sites built after the crisis (HM-03 NW of Carol City, HM-40 North Key Largo, HM-66, HM-69 completed 1964, HM-95 SW Miami), active until 1979. The South Florida Nike sites used above-ground missile 'barns' because the water table is too high for bunkers
Air operations supplemented from the former Marine Corps Air Station at Opa-locka

beats.what: U-2 photographs missile sites in Cuba
Jets pour into Homestead; convoys; tents; HAWK launchers appear
JFK visits Homestead AFB to view the build-up
Permanent Nike Hercules sites (HM-69 completed 1964; the batteries stayed until 1979)

effects: pairs of swept-wing F-100 jets climbing south over the bay
missile launchers on the city's edge
do_not_show: missiles being fired or jets attacking: no shots were fired

sequences.title: Civil unrest (1968, 1980, 1982, 1989)
sequences.type: civil unrest, NOT war. Animate respectfully: no combat choreography
sequences.in_main_frame: Overtown yes; Liberty City is just north of the main frame

events.place: Liberty City (during the Republican National Convention in Miami Beach)
Overtown, Liberty City, Brownsville, West Coconut Grove and nearby
events.facts: Began after the acquittal of officers in Arthur McDuffie's death. 18 killed, 350-370 injured, 600-787 arrested, over $100 million in damage. National Guard: 500, then 1,000, then 2,500 more (3,500 total). Curfew 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.
Began after a police shooting; 1 additional death
Began after officer William Lozano shot motorcyclist Clement Lloyd; passenger Allen Blanchard died the next day; no deaths in the riot; 13 businesses burned

sequences.suggested_treatment: Smoke columns rising from the neighbourhood, streets going dark for the curfew, National Guard trucks on the arterials, a sober caption. No figures fighting.

sequences.title: Mariel boatlift
sequences.in_main_frame: arrival scenes only; most boats landed at Key West, off-map
sequences.facts: April 15 to October 31, 1980. About 125,000 Cubans in about 1,700 boats from Mariel Harbor, Cuba; the first boat docked at Key West on April 21. About 25,000 Haitians also arrived in the same period. In Miami, the Orange Bowl was used as a temporary refuge, then a tent city under I-95 near downtown (closed late September 1980)

approach.to: Key West mainly, then overland to Miami

effects: flotilla of small overloaded boats (inset map or horizon shot)
tents in the Orange Bowl and under the I-95 overpass

locations.name: Tent City under I-95 near downtown
